abstract: Using a novel dataset of AI publications merged with Burning Glass vacancy data (2007-2019), the authors examine whether geographic distance from AI innovation hotspots slows AI adoption across 741 US commuting zones. They find that distance from innovation is a significant barrier, with effects driven by proximity to AI research papers rather than patents, and amplified by state borders.
keyFindings: A commuting zone 200km farther from the closest AI hotspot has 17% lower growth in AI jobs' share of vacancies over seven years
The distance effect is driven by proximity to AI research papers, not AI patents
State borders between commuting zones and their closest hotspot explain 20% of the overall distance effect
Distance reduces growth in both AI research jobs and jobs adapting AI to new industries (e.g., finance and insurance)
Distance has much less impact on downstream AI adoption (e.g., use of image processing) than on AI adaptation and development
methodology: Novel dataset combining Microsoft Academic Graph AI publications with Burning Glass Technologies (Lightcast) online job vacancy data, aggregated to 741 US commuting zones from 2007-2019. AI innovation hotspots defined by cumulative pre-period AI publication counts. AI adoption measured by share of job vacancies requiring AI skills.
qualifiers: Covers 2007-2019 period, prior to the generative AI era (ChatGPT launched Nov 2022). Uses job postings as a proxy for AI adoption, which may not capture informal or unposted AI use. US-only data. The distinction between AI 'adaptation' (developing new AI applications) and 'adoption' (using existing AI tools) is important: distance mainly affects the former.
